title: Stance: how to stand on the shooting stand
summary: Feet, weight, knees and body turn: a simple, compact stance that lets you move the gun smoothly with the target.

body.html: The stance is how the shooter stands before the shot. The space is small: in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the stand is a 1 m square or circle, and both feet must be inside it before the call. In Compak® Sporting each station is a 1 m square with a Firing Angle Limiter, a frame that stops the shooter stepping forward and limits the swing.
The front foot points at the break point; the body winds back to the hold point.
body.heading: Watch the stance

body.html: The key instruction: point your front foot at the break point, the spot where you plan to break the target. Then your body is relaxed and faces the right way at the moment you fire. Before you call, turn your upper body back from the hips towards the hold point, the place where the barrels wait for the target. When the target flies, you simply turn back the way you came, like a spring unwinding. If your feet point at the trap instead, coaches warn, your body cannot turn far enough to reach the break point, and the gun stops or your head comes up.

The usual base: feet about shoulder-width apart, and for a right-hander the left foot slightly forward (a left-hander mirrors this). Knees are soft, not locked. The weight is slightly forward, roughly 60 per cent on the front foot. Coaches say “nose over toes”.
The body turns from the hips, not the arms. Feet may be set slightly differently for each target.
A good stance keeps you balanced while the body turns with the target. Leaning slightly forward also helps you take the recoil instead of being rocked back; see Recoil, shoulder and neck.
Safety comes before comfort. Stay inside the stand, and open and unload the gun before you turn round on it. This rule is the same in both disciplines.

A stance is not a pose for a photo. A coach will watch how you stand and correct the details: foot width, angle and lean. This lesson explains the basics; learn the technique itself with a qualified coach.

notes.html: Translate “front foot” and “back foot” as front and back, not left and right: your shooter may be left-handed.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Point your front foot at the break point.
phrases.meaning: Turn the toe of the front foot towards the place where the target will be broken.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Set your feet for the break, then wind back to the hold.
phrases.meaning: First place the feet for the break point, then turn the upper body back to the hold point.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Lean slightly onto the front foot and do not lock the knees.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Turn from the hips, not the arms.
phrases.meaning: The whole upper body rotates; the arms do not swing the gun on their own.

key_points.html: Front foot points at the break point; turn back from the hips to the hold point.
Feet shoulder-width, knees soft, weight slightly forward.
Sporting™: both feet inside the 1 m stand before the call.
Compak® Sporting: 1 m station with a Firing Angle Limiter.
Open and unload the gun before you turn round on the stand.

did_you_know.html: On a Compak® Sporting station the Firing Angle Limiter is often a simple frame of coloured plastic tubes. It limits how far the gun can swing sideways, up and down.

quiz.q: Where does the coach usually want the front foot to point?
quiz.explain: Feet set to the break point keep the body relaxed where the shot happens. If the feet face the trap, the body cannot turn far enough to reach the break point.

quiz.q: What do the Sporting™ rules require of the feet before the call?

options.text: The front foot on the stand line

quiz.explain: The ready-position rule asks for both feet inside the 1 m shooting stand before the shooter calls.

quiz.q: A left-handed shooter. The coach says “Open your front foot”. Which foot is it?

options.text: The left one, whatever the hand
The right one: a left-hander's front foot
The back foot, nearer the trap

quiz.explain: For a left-hander the front foot is the right one. Translating “front foot” as front, not as left, avoids the mistake.
